newsitem.title: USA: USDA sees potential for US meat exports to China.
newsitem.headline: USDA sees potential for US meat exports to China.

text.p: U.S. beef and pork exports to China could grow rapidly over the next several years if current market barriers are removed, a U.S. Agriculture Department official said Wednesday.
"The outlook for meat trade to China depends on broadening market access for meats," said James Parker, USDA Foreign Agricultural Service deputy administrator for commodity and marketing programs.

The United States continues to insist that China make "meaningful concessions," such as reducing tariffs on meat imports and removing other barriers, in the ongoing negotiations on China's bid to join the World Trade Organization, Parker said.
"It is critical that China subscribe to the same rules as other countries who are in the WTO," he told a House Agriculture subcommittee.

The combination of China's 45 percent tariff rate on imported pork and its complicated and secretive import regulations amount to a "de facto ban on pork imports" John Hardin, representing the National Pork Producer Council, told the farm panel.

To the great frustration of the U.S pork industry, Chinese quarantine officials have so far refused to supply copies of their pork import restrictions on the grounds that "the laws are confidential," Hardin said.
China's quarantine administration last month set quotas providing limited access to its retail pork market under a one-year trial program for U.S., Australian and Canadian meat and poultry exporters.
In the past, China has only allowed meat imports for its restaurant and hotel sector.

But it is doubtful that "significant" shipments will occur under the quotas -- 2,000 tonnes for Australia, 5,500 tonnes for the United States and 68,000 tonnes for Canada -- because of the high tariffs and other restrictive barriers that remain, Hardin said.
Chuck Lambert, chief economist of the National Cattlemen's Beef Association, also stressed that China be required to provide increased market access before joining the WTO.
But "unlike pork and poultry, there is no well-established domestic beef industry in China, which should minimize protectionist issues with respect to beef," he said.

Also, after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese control at the end of June, China will be the fifth largest market for U.S. beef with total imports of nearly $68 million in 1996, he said, assuming Hong Kong import rules remain the same.
As with pork, China has also recently approved a limited number of U.S beef plants for direct export to China's private sector, Lambert said.
But that is only a first step toward providing meaningful market access, he said.
Meanwhile, the stunning increase in U.S. poultry exports to China over the past decades indicates what the future could hold for beef and pork, Parker said.
China is one of the fastest growing markets for poultry meat with imports of nearly $500 million from the United States in 1996, Parker said.
Nevertheless, China's high tariffs and import restrictions also thwart U.S poultry sales, B.M "Bob" Anthony, chairman of American Poultry Ltd., told the farm panel.
"We would like to see a much more transparent import program for poultry so that we, as exporters, can better gauge our risks and market potential," Anthony said.
"Too often rules change in mid-stream and change somewhat capriciously," he said.
